title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Setup
Inline completion is the most familiar AI coding feature: grey “ghost text” appears as you type, suggesting a continuation. You accept with Tab, reject with Esc, or ignore it by carrying on typing. This block teaches what context inline completion uses, and the practical consequence: what you write immediately before the cursor matters more than anything else.
⏱ ~35 minutes
Use one completion provider at a time during this block, so you know which tool produced each suggestion.
Check it works: open a blank R script and type # Calculate the mean of 1 to 100. Within a second or two you should see ghost text such as mean(1:100). If nothing appears, press Enter to move to the next line and wait.
Copilot Free allows a limited number of completions per month (2,000 at the time of writing); paid Copilot plans and Posit AI do not meter completions. Completions send the code around your cursor to the provider, so the disclosure points in the context-and-disclosure block apply here too.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
RStudio: either GitHub Copilot (enable it in RStudio’s options and sign in to GitHub) or Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions (from the Posit Assistant toolbar button; requires a Posit AI account).

Positron: completions come from Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions or GitHub Copilot. See Positron’s completions documentation for how to choose and toggle the provider.

VS Code: Copilot’s AI features are built in. Select Use AI Features from the Copilot icon in the Status Bar and sign in with GitHub.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
The context principle
What an inline suggestion is based on depends on the provider:


GitHub Copilot works mainly from the current file: the code above and below the cursor, and especially the comment immediately before it. In Positron and VS Code it may also draw on other open tabs. It does not see your R session.

Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions also sees your live R session: the columns of loaded data frames, functions you have defined and packages you have loaded.

The practical consequence for both: the comment immediately before your cursor, and the code above it, have the largest effect on what you get. A session-aware provider adds one more lever: what you have loaded.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Activity: The context demonstration


The context demonstration


You will use voles_metabolism.csv, a small synthetic dataset chosen because its column names are unlikely to appear in any model’s training data. The columns are subject_id, sex, treatment_arm, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g and metabolic_rate_post. The data record a hypothetical metabolism trial in 72 voles, with three treatment arms and two sexes.


1. No context. Restart R so that nothing is loaded. Open a blank R script, type only this comment, and wait:

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment

Record the suggestion. With no library() call, no data and no column names visible, the model has to guess. Expect something syntactically plausible but wrong for this dataset.
2. Context in the file. Start a new blank script and add:

# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
# 72 voles, three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose), two sexes
# Native pipe |>, tidyverse

library(tidyverse)

voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))
glimpse(voles)

Then add the same comment as before on a new line:

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment

Record the suggestion. A typical good result:


Solution


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(
    mean_change = mean(mass_change_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = treatment_arm
  )


The exact form varies between people and sessions; that variation is itself part of the lesson.
3. Posit AI only: context in the session. Run the lines from step 2 so that voles exists in your session. Then open a new, blank script, type only the comment from step 1, and wait. If the suggestion now uses the real column names, it came from your session, not from the file.
How different were the outputs? Did the later versions use column names that exist in the data? Did the model compute the change in the right direction (post minus pre)?

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Activity: Build a small analysis


Build a small analysis


In the script from step 2, drive inline completion through a four-step analysis. Write the comment for each step first, then accept, reject or modify the suggestion.
1. Filter to subjects with non-missing metabolic_rate_post and create a derived variable mass_change_g.
2. Produce a summary table of the mean and standard deviation of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with the number of observations per cell.
3. Fit a linear model of metabolic_rate_post on treatment_arm and sex. Inspect the coefficients.
4. Produce one plot relating mass_change_g to metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm.
For each step, record the comment you wrote, the suggested code, and one line saying whether you accepted, modified or rejected it. The point of the record is to make you notice when you accepted something without inspecting it.
Work in pairs. Each partner attempts steps 2 and 4 independently before comparing. Comparison usually surfaces different suggestions, different acceptance decisions and, often, different bugs.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Check your understanding
The single most reliable way to improve inline suggestions in a new script is to:

Switch to a different underlying modelOpen more files in the editor as additional contextWrite a specific comment immediately before the code you want, naming the data frame and its columnsRestart the IDE so the assistant has a fresh context

You get correct column names in a blank script using Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions, but not with Copilot. The most likely reason is:

Posit AI uses a larger modelNext Edit Suggestions can see the data frame loaded in your R session; Copilot sees only the filesCopilot cannot read R codeThe column names were in Posit AI's training data

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Setup
AI is most useful for debugging code you wrote yourself. You know what you intended, so you can judge its diagnosis against your intention rather than against an unknown ground truth. It can spot syntax mistakes you missed, suggest fixes for errors, and explain unfamiliar messages.
This block uses four error types, ordered by what the debugger needs to know. The first is a typo that needs no data. The second needs the actual values in the data. The third needs ggplot2’s grammar. The fourth runs cleanly, returns a plausible answer and is wrong; only knowledge of the expected result reveals it. The differences show where AI can stand in for looking up documentation, where it cannot stand in for inspecting the data, and where it cannot stand in for knowing the biology.
⏱ ~30 minutes
Load the voles data:
library(tidyverse)
voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))
Use whichever assistant you have: inline completion, a chat window, Posit Assistant or Claude Code. Where a step depends on the tool, it says so.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 1: A syntax error
You wrote this to count voles per treatment:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_barchart()

R returns:
Error in geom_barchart(): could not find function "geom_barchart"
1. Ask for a fix. With inline completion, paste the code and the error into your script as a block comment, add # Fix this code:, and let the assistant suggest a continuation. With a chat window or agent, paste both and ask.

# This code gives an error:
# ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
#   geom_barchart()
#
# Error: could not find function "geom_barchart"
#
# Fix this code:

Before accepting any suggestion, write one sentence explaining why the original failed. That sentence is your verification step: if you can write it, you understood the fix; if you cannot, the AI has solved the problem and you have learned nothing.


Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_bar()

The function is geom_bar(), not geom_barchart(). ggplot2’s geoms use short names with no _chart suffix. “Could not find function” is R’s standard message when a function does not exist in any loaded package, and it is the easiest class of error to recognise.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 2: A logic error
You wrote this to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles:

high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

The code runs without error and returns:
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_mass
      <dbl>
1       NaN
There is no error message to paste. The code does exactly what you asked; the bug is in what you asked for. No assistant can diagnose this reliably without knowing what your data contain.
1. Inspect the data before asking for help. Three calls take seconds:

voles |> distinct(treatment_arm)
voles |> count(treatment_arm)
nrow(high_dose)

The first two show that the values are Control, Low_dose and High_dose (capital first letter, underscore between words). The third returns zero. You have diagnosed the bug without an AI.
2. Ask with the evidence in hand. Paste the code and the diagnostic output together and ask for confirmation:
I am trying to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles.
My code:

  high_dose <- voles |>
    filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

  high_dose |>
    summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

returns NaN. But voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) returns
"Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose". I think the filter fails because of
the capitalisation. Is that the only problem?
The exercise is to ask with the diagnostic context already in place, not to ask the AI to diagnose blind. AI is quick at typo-spotting and syntax recall; distinct() is quicker at telling you what is in your data.
With an agent (Posit Assistant or Claude Code), you can ask it to run the diagnostics itself. Ask it to show the commands and their output, and read the output yourself before accepting its diagnosis.


Solution


high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "High_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g, na.rm = TRUE))

The value now matches the data exactly. na.rm = TRUE is a precaution: this dataset has no missing values in mass_post_g, but real biological data usually do.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 3: An aesthetic-mapping error
You wanted a scatter plot of post-treatment metabolic rate against post-treatment mass, coloured by treatment arm:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(color = treatment_arm) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

R returns an error saying that object treatment_arm was not found. The exact wording varies between ggplot2 versions.
1. Ask for a fix. Before accepting it, write one sentence on why ggplot2 could not find treatment_arm.


Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = treatment_arm)) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

treatment_arm is a column in the data, so the mapping must go inside aes(). An argument outside aes(), such as color =, expects a fixed value like "red" or "#0072B2". ggplot2 looked for an object called treatment_arm in your environment, found none, and stopped. colour and color are interchangeable in ggplot2.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
section: Exercise 4: A correct-looking but wrong result
text:
Exercise 4: A correct-looking but wrong result
You want the mean change in body mass by treatment arm:

voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

It runs. There is no error and no NaN. It returns something like:
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  treatment_arm mean_change
  <chr>               <dbl>
1 Control             -0.21
2 Low_dose            -1.49
3 High_dose           -3.19
Every value is a small number of grams, plausible for a vole, so nothing looks wrong. But the result is the reverse of the truth. The treatment was designed to increase body mass, and the dataset was built so that mass rises with dose. The table says that mass falls, and falls most at the highest dose.
The data are clean, so glimpse(), distinct() and count() report nothing unusual. The fault is in the arithmetic: mass_pre_g - mass_post_g measures loss, when you wanted gain.






Note



Can an AI catch this? Only if it knows what the answer should be. Given the code and output alone, an assistant can describe what the code does, but nothing in the code or the output says that mass should rise. If you state the expected direction, it is far more likely to name the error. The knowledge that makes the error visible is yours.


1. Before you trust any result that runs cleanly, write down what a correct result should look like. Here: positive values, increasing from Control to High_dose. Then compare. The mismatch between “positive and increasing” and “negative and decreasing” is the diagnosis.
2. You may ask an AI for a second opinion, with the expected direction included. “This should show mass gain increasing with dose, but the values are negative and decreasing; what is wrong?” will usually get the sign error named. A prompt with only the code and output usually will not.


Solution


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

mass_change_g is post minus pre. With the subtraction the right way round, the means are positive and increase with dose, matching the study design. The original ran without complaint because subtraction works in either direction; the only signal that it was wrong was knowing what the answer should be.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
The debugging checklist
When code fails, order matters: inspect the data first, ask the AI second.


Read the error message in full. The function name and the phrase (“could not find function”, “object not found”, “non-numeric argument”) usually locate the bug.

Inspect the relevant data. glimpse(), distinct() on categorical columns, summary() on numeric columns, and nrow() after a filter catch most logic errors in seconds.

Check names exactly, including capitalisation and underscores. Most “object not found” errors are typos.

If steps 1 to 3 do not locate the bug, give the assistant the code, the error message and the diagnostic output together. The combination is much more useful than the error alone.

After the AI suggests a fix, write one sentence explaining why the original failed. If you cannot, you have not understood the fix.

Before trusting a result that runs without error, state what it should look like (sign, rough magnitude, expected ordering) and compare. This check depends on your knowledge of the study, which no assistant has unless you supply it.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Check your understanding
When ggplot2 reports that a column such as treatment_arm was not found, the most common cause is:

The data argument was supplied incorrectlyA column name was used outside aes(), where ggplot2 expected a fixed valueThe ggplot2 package is not loadedThe variable contains missing values

Code runs without error and returns plausible numbers. What is the most reliable first check?

Ask an AI whether the code is correctRun the code again to confirm the output is stableWrite down what the result should look like from the study design, then compareCheck that there are no warnings

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Part A: What can the assistant see?
Two questions decide how far you can trust anything an AI assistant does with your code:
This block covers both, using the three tools in this course: Claude Code in the terminal, Posit Assistant in RStudio or Positron, and GitHub Copilot, both in the browser and as an asynchronous cloud agent.
⏱ ~55 minutes

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Exercise 1: Context decides the answer


The same error, three levels of context (15 minutes)


1. Error only. In a browser chat, open a fresh session and paste only this, asking “What does this error mean?”:
Error in `mutate()`:
ℹ In argument: `mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g`.
Caused by error:
! object 'mass_post' not found
The answer can only reason from the error text.
2. Error plus code plus structure. In a new session, paste:
I am running this code:

  voles |>
    mutate(mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g)

and getting:

  Error in `mutate()`:
  ℹ In argument: `mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g`.
  Caused by error:
  ! object 'mass_post' not found

The data structure is:

  Rows: 72
  Columns: 6
  $ subject_id          <chr> "V001", "V002", "V003", ...
  $ sex                 <chr> "M", "F", "M", ...
  $ treatment_arm       <chr> "Control", "Control", ...
  $ mass_pre_g          <dbl> 28.3, 27.9, 30.1, ...
  $ mass_post_g         <dbl> 28.5, 28.0, 30.5, ...
  $ metabolic_rate_post <dbl> 13.21, 12.84, 13.55, ...

What is wrong?
It should name the missing _g suffix.
3. No paste at all. Load the data in your R session, run the failing code, then ask Posit Assistant (or Claude Code, from the project folder) only: “Why did my last command fail?” A session-aware assistant can read your console history and the data frame; Claude Code can open the script and run code to inspect the data.
Then ask: “How do you know the column names?” Compare its answer with what you know it was given. If it claims to have seen something it could not have seen, you have found the unreliability described in the callout above.


The lesson is not that one route is correct. The answer is only as good as the context, and context reaches the model by more than one route.

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
section: Disclosure: every route out of your machine
text:
Disclosure: every route out of your machine
Everything an assistant sees is sent to a model provider. Data leave your machine by four routes:


What you paste. Errors, outputs, printed results.

Files it reads. A data file in the repository or project folder.

Session context the IDE injects. Posit Assistant reads loaded packages, data frames and console history, so a data frame in memory can reach the model without any paste.

Output of commands it runs. If an agent runs print(voles) or head data.csv, those values enter its context.

Before you decide what to show, know what the surface can already reach. A data file committed to the repository, or a tibble loaded in your session, may already be disclosed.
When you describe a data frame deliberately, three commands reveal increasing amounts:


names(voles) lists column names only, in their original order.

summary(voles) adds ranges, quartiles and missing-value counts for numeric columns: the shape of the data, not individual records.

glimpse(voles) or str(voles) adds the first few actual values of every column.







Important



Before using an assistant on research data, check three things: whether your institution permits sending this kind of data to this provider; whether your ethics approval and data-sharing agreements allow it; and whether a synthetic or anonymised copy would serve instead. Tool settings that restrict reading (see the enforced-controls block) reduce accidental exposure, but they do not make an agent safe for confidential data: any command it runs that prints data sends that data to the provider.

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
section: Exercise 2: Context you hold in your head
text:
Exercise 2: Context you hold in your head


Refine an approach question (10 minutes)


1. In a fresh browser chat, ask exactly:
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
With no design and no question supplied, you will get a tour of options (paired tests, change scores, ANCOVA, mixed models) rather than a recommendation.
2. In a new session, state the design and the question:
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to
control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside
any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary
analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
3. Compare the answers. A data file can supply column names and types, but not your scientific question or your design intent. Those exist only in your head until you write them down.
Treat even the better answer as a proposal to check against a statistics text or a colleague. Choosing the primary analysis is your decision, not the assistant’s.

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
section: Exercise 3: The same task, rising autonomy
text:
Exercise 3: The same task, rising autonomy


Ask, plan, act (20 minutes)


Use your forked workshop repository, committed and clean, so every change is a diff you can inspect or revert. Never run an agent with uncommitted work you are not prepared to lose.
1. Ask. At rung 1, ask:
In scripts/clean_voles.R, how would I add a column mass_change equal to
mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g?
Read the answer. Confirm with git status that nothing changed.
2. Plan. At rung 2, give a goal that spans several files:
In the voles pipeline, add a derived mass_change column (mass_post_g minus
mass_pre_g) in the cleaning step, create a new script that plots mass_change
by treatment_arm, and make sure the pipeline still runs end to end.
Before approving, check that the plan names every file it will touch, does not touch raw data, says where the plot script goes, and says how it will check the pipeline runs. Amend the plan in conversation if any of that is missing.
3. Act, with approval. Approve the plan and stay at rung 3. Read each approval prompt before answering it. Refuse at least one action you consider out of scope, and note how the agent responds.
4. Review. When it finishes:
git status
git diff
Read the diff as you would a colleague’s contribution. The agent’s statement that the pipeline “still runs” is a claim; run the pipeline yourself to check it.
5. Compare. At which rung did you decide the most? At which rung would you have missed an unwanted change if you had not read the diff?
The asynchronous rung, the Copilot cloud agent, is demonstrated in the characterisation-test block, where its pull request meets a review gate.








Note



Access and cost. Plans and prices change; check before the session.


Claude Code needs an Anthropic account, used through a subscription or an API key; see Anthropic’s documentation for current options.

Posit Assistant uses Posit AI Pass or your own provider key, including an Anthropic API key. In RStudio, providers are configured in the assistant’s settings.

GitHub Copilot bills in AI credits. Copilot Free includes only limited agent features. Check GitHub’s plans page to see whether your plan includes the cloud agent.

Your institution may have approved some of these tools and not others.

Nothing; both see only what you pasteYour live R session, including loaded packages, data frames in memory and console history, without your pasting anythingEvery file on your computerThe data of other users of the same tool

In Claude Code’s acceptEdits mode, what does the agent do without asking?

Nothing; acceptEdits only changes how diffs are displayedOnly edits to files you have namedIt edits files and runs common file commands such as cp and mv without asking, but still asks before other shell commandsEverything, including all shell commands

Which check still works whatever rung the agent ran at?

The agent's own report that the task succeededThe approval prompts you saw during the sessionInspecting the changes with git status and git diff, and running the code yourselfThe plan the agent proposed before starting

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Part A: Instructions
The previous block showed that the further up the autonomy ladder an assistant works, the more its unstated assumptions land in your files. This block is how you state your conventions once, so you do not repeat them in every prompt.
There are two mechanisms, distinguished by when they load:
Both are requests. The model usually follows them, but nothing guarantees it. Rules that must hold every time belong in the enforced controls of the next block.
⏱ ~55 minutes

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Where each tool looks








File
Claude Code
Posit Assistant
GitHub Copilot




AGENTS.md (repository root)
Via an import in CLAUDE.md

Read as project memory
Read by the cloud agent, agent mode and the CLI


CLAUDE.md
Read every session
—
Read by the cloud agent


.github/copilot-instructions.md

Read by Copilot; also offered for conversion by /import-instructions in Posit Assistant


Path-scoped rules

.claude/rules/*.md with paths

No equivalent found

.github/instructions/*.instructions.md with applyTo




This course uses one source of truth: conventions live in AGENTS.md, and CLAUDE.md contains a single line that imports it:
@AGENTS.md
Copilot’s cloud agent reads both files, so it may see the conventions twice. That is harmless but wasteful, so keep CLAUDE.md to that one line.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Writing instructions that work


One instruction per line. Short, concrete statements are easier to check than paragraphs, for the model and for you.

Describe what you actually do. An instruction your existing code breaks sends the model mixed signals. The test is whether your own scripts obey it.

Be specific. “Use the native pipe |>” can be checked; “write clean, idiomatic code” cannot.

Keep it short. The file loads into every request. Anthropic advises keeping Claude Code’s always-loaded file under about 200 lines; aim far lower.

Add a rule when a mistake repeats. If the assistant gets the same convention wrong twice, that convention belongs in the file. A one-off correction in chat is forgotten next session.

Do not put guarantees here. “Never edit raw data” is worth stating, but enforce it with the controls in the next block.



Example AGENTS.md

# Project conventions: voles analysis

## Canary
When you write or edit R code, make the first line of the first code block:
# agents-md: active v1

## Structure
- Raw data live in data/raw/ and are never modified.
- Derived data go to data/derived/; figures and tables go to outputs/.
- Reusable functions live in scripts/functions/.

## R style
- Tidyverse style, native pipe |>, snake_case names, <- for assignment.
- Write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F.
- Build every path with here::here(). Never use setwd() or rm(list = ls()).
- Read CSV files with readr and explicit col_types.

## Reproducibility
- Packages are managed with renv. Do not call install.packages(); ask before
  adding a package.
- Set a seed immediately before any random step.
- Every script must run in a fresh R session.

## Data integrity
- Never drop rows silently; state the reason for every filter in a comment.
- Report the number of observations behind every summary statistic.

## Statistics
- Label each analysis as exploratory or confirmatory.
- Never type numerical results into text; compute them in code.

## Working with me
- Before changing more than one file, present a plan and wait for approval.
- Do not edit anything under data/raw/, tests/fixtures/ or .github/.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
section: Activity: Build and test your AGENTS.md
text:
Activity: Build and test your AGENTS.md


Write, trim, verify (20 minutes)


Work in your forked workshop repository, committed and clean.
1. Baseline. With no AGENTS.md present, ask your assistant (rung 1, Ask):
Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot of
mass_post_g by treatment arm.
Keep the answer.
2. Draft. Ask the assistant to draft an AGENTS.md by reading the repository. In Posit Assistant you can instead have a short conversation about your conventions and run /savememory. Expect the draft to be long and generic.
3. Trim hard. Delete anything the model padded or guessed. Keep only what is always true of this project.
4. Make it yours. Make sure the file states at least:

one style convention you genuinely follow and the draft did not infer;
one structural fact the model cannot guess, such as where raw data live and that they are immutable;
one reproducibility or statistical convention you always apply;
a canary: a fixed first line for any R code block, such as # agents-md: active v1.

5. Connect Claude Code. Create CLAUDE.md containing only @AGENTS.md.
6. Verify in each tool you use. Commit, open a new session, and repeat the Step 1 prompt.

If the canary appears, the file is being loaded.
If the canary is missing, the file is not reaching that tool. Check the file location, that the change is committed (for the Copilot cloud agent, pushed to the default branch), and, in Posit Assistant, that you trusted the workspace.
A canary shows that the file was loaded, not that every rule was followed. Check the plot code against each rule you wrote.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
section: Activity: A rule for Quarto files only
text:
Activity: A rule for Quarto files only
Some rules are right for one kind of file and wrong elsewhere. A chunk option such as #| echo: false is meaningful in a .qmd file and meaningless in an .R script. The test for a scoped rule: would it be wrong, not merely irrelevant, in the files it excludes? If not, put it in AGENTS.md.


Create and test a scoped rule (10 minutes)


The rules themselves:
# Quarto document conventions

- Set chunk options with the hashpipe (#|) inside the chunk, not in the
  {r} header.
- Give every chunk a label; prefix figure chunks with fig-.
- Every figure chunk sets #| fig-cap:, #| fig-width: and #| fig-height:.
- Refer to figures in the text with @fig-..., never by a typed number.
- Default to #| echo: false unless the document is a code walkthrough.
- Resolve paths with here::here(); never assume the working directory is the
  document's folder.
Place them where your tool looks:


Copilot: .github/instructions/quarto.instructions.md, beginning with this front matter:
---
applyTo: "**/*.qmd"
---


Claude Code: .claude/rules/quarto.md, beginning with front matter that restricts it to Quarto files:
---
paths:
  - "**/*.qmd"
---

Posit Assistant: no path-scoped instruction file is documented. Add the rules to AGENTS.md under a heading such as “When editing .qmd files”, or rely on its built-in quarto-authoring skill.

Test. Open a .qmd file and ask for a chunk that plots mass_post_g by treatment_arm. A correct answer uses hashpipe options, a fig- label, a caption and here::here(). Then ask for the same plot in an .R script; the Quarto rules should not appear. If they do not appear in the .qmd either, the rule is not loading on your surface. Report what you found; behaviour differs between tools.


Every scoped rule is a second copy of a convention to keep in step, once per tool. Use scoped rules sparingly.

mkdir -p .claude/skills

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
section: Activity: Write a skill and test it
text:
Activity: Write a skill and test it


A house figure style (20 minutes)


1. Create .agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md:
---
name: house-figures
description: >-
  Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear
  in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a
  figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots.
---

# House figure style

## Rules
1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation
   (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar
   with error bars ("dynamite plot").
2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette
   (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same
   variable to point shape so the figure works without colour.
3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)".
4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12).
5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure.
6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a
   fitted model and asks for them.

## Before returning code
List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why.
2. Without the skill. In a session where the skill is not invoked, ask:
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report.
3. With the skill. In a new session, invoke it by name (/house-figures) and ask the same thing.
4. Grade it. For each of the six rules, record whether the output complies:


Rule
Without skill
With skill



1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot




2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape




3. Units in axis titles




4. theme_classic(base_size = 12)





5. n per group shown




6. No unrequested p-values





Run the code and look at the figure. Code that names the right functions can still produce the wrong picture.
5. Test the trigger. Without naming the skill, ask “Give me a quick look at mass_post_g by arm” (exploratory, so the skill should not load), then “Polish this figure for the poster” (it should load). If either goes the wrong way, rewrite the description and test again.
6. Test a rule under pressure. Ask the assistant to “add significance stars between the groups”. Rule 6 says it should decline without a fitted model. Note whether it did. A skill is an instruction, not a guarantee.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Skills you did not write
Each tool ships built-in skills. Claude Code bundles skills such as /code-review and /debug. Posit Assistant includes quarto-authoring and r-package-development. Collections of shared skills are published online, for example Anthropic’s anthropics/skills repository.
Before installing a skill someone else wrote, read it. A skill can include scripts that the assistant may run on your machine, and its instructions shape what the assistant does with your files and data. Treat it as you would any code from the internet.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Check your understanding
Your canary line appears in Claude Code’s answers but not in Posit Assistant’s. What is the most likely explanation?

Posit Assistant cannot follow instructionsThe instruction file is not reaching Posit Assistant, for example because the workspace is untrusted or the file is not where it looksThe canary only works with Anthropic modelsAGENTS.md must be renamed CLAUDE.md for Posit Assistant

What is the essential difference between an instruction file and a skill?

Instruction files can contain code; skills cannotInstructions load into every session automatically; a skill loads only when invoked by name or judged relevant from its descriptionSkills are enforced; instructions are advisoryInstruction files work only with Copilot

A skill fires for quick exploratory plots when you meant it only for publication figures. What should you change first?

The rules in the body of the skillThe description, so it states precisely when the skill applies and when it does notThe folder the skill is stored inThe model you are using

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates
text:
Layers of control
Everything you have written so far to steer an assistant (custom instructions, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, skills) is a request. The model reads it and usually follows it, but nothing guarantees that it will. Anthropic’s own documentation for Claude Code makes the same distinction: a “never edit this file” line in an instruction file is a request, while a hook that blocks the edit is enforcement.
For research code, a few things must hold every time: raw data are never modified, a frozen reference output is never regenerated by the code it is meant to check, and the checks themselves are not quietly edited to pass. This block builds the controls that make those rules hold, and shows you where each control stops working.
The protections you build here are reused in the data-cleaning and characterisation-test blocks.
⏱ ~50 minutes
Two principles follow from the table:

Test every control. A control you have not seen refuse something is a control you are assuming.

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates
text:
Exercise 1: What needs protecting?


Threat-model your repository (5 minutes)


For the workshop repository, list each asset, what could go wrong, and how you would notice. Start from this table and add to it:







Asset
What could go wrong
How you would notice

Overwritten or “tidied” in place

Reference output regenerated by the code under test

A failing test edited until it passes

The last two rows are easy to miss. Configuration files that hold your controls are themselves assets: an agent that can edit its settings can remove its own restrictions.

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates
text:
Exercise 2: Permission rules
Claude Code
Permission rules live in .claude/settings.json, which is committed and shared with everyone who uses the repository:
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Edit(/.posit/**)",
      "Edit(/hooks/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}
A leading / anchors the pattern to the project root. Edit rules apply to all of Claude Code’s built-in file-editing tools; use Edit, not Write, for path rules.
Posit Assistant
Posit Assistant’s permissions are set per tool in .posit/assistant/settings.json, with pattern matching for shell commands:
{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "rm *": "deny"
    },
    "edit": "ask"
  }
}
deny rules are enforced in every approval mode, including auto and YOLO. The documentation does not describe path patterns for file edits, so protection of specific paths comes from the hook in Exercise 3. Posit Assistant blocks reading .env and .Renviron by default.


Test the rule, then find the gap (10 minutes)


Work in the practice repository, not on real data. Create a scratch file data/raw/canary.csv containing one line, and commit it.
1. Confirm the rule refuses. Ask your assistant:
Add a second line, "test", to data/raw/canary.csv.
In Claude Code, the edit should be refused. Run /permissions to see which rule refused it.
2. Find the gap. Now ask:
Run this R code: writeLines(c("a", "test"), "data/raw/canary.csv")
Claude Code’s deny rules apply to its built-in file tools, not to commands it runs through the shell or R. What stops this second request? In normal mode, the approval prompt: you are asked before the command runs. In a mode that auto-approves commands, nothing in this exercise does.
3. Detect it. Whatever happened, run:
git status --short data/raw
If the file changed, git shows it. Restore it with git restore data/raw/canary.csv.

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates
crumbs: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates
text:
Exercise 4: Break your own guard


Red-team the tripwire (5 minutes)


Ask the assistant to run:
Run this R code:
writeLines(c("a", "test"), here::here("data", "raw", "canary.csv"))
The guard searches for the text data/raw. This call never contains it, because here::here() assembles the path from separate pieces, so the guard allows the call. A Windows path written with backslashes would also slip past.
This is the general limit of hooks that match text: they catch the obvious form of a dangerous action, not every way of expressing it. Claude Code’s documentation makes the same point about command patterns. A guard hook is a tripwire that stops accidents and makes intent visible; it is not a wall. git status still catches the change. Restore the file before moving on.

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates
section: Exercise 5: The review gate on GitHub
text:
Exercise 5: The review gate on GitHub
Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely, such as the Copilot cloud agent. There, the controls are on the repository itself.
1. CODEOWNERS. Create .github/CODEOWNERS on your default branch:
/data/raw/            @your-github-username
/tests/               @your-github-username
/.github/             @your-github-username
/hooks/               @your-github-username
/.claude/             @your-github-username
/.posit/              @your-github-username
Code owners are requested for review automatically when a pull request changes the files they own. CODEOWNERS works in public repositories on free plans; for private repositories it requires a paid plan.
2. Branch protection. In the repository settings, add a rule for main that requires a pull request before merging, requires review from code owners, and requires the r-checks status check to pass.
3. Test it. Open a pull request that changes a file under tests/, for example by asking the Copilot cloud agent to “update the test to use a tolerance of 1e-6”. Confirm that the pull request cannot merge until you have reviewed it.
GitHub does not let you approve your own pull request. In a repository where you are the only person, a pull request you open yourself may need an administrator override, which is a reason to test this gate with an agent’s pull request.
crumbs: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates
section: Feedback hooks: useful, with a warning
text:
Feedback hooks: useful, with a warning
Hooks can do more than block. A PostToolUse hook can run lintr on each R file the agent edits and pass the result back to it. A Stop hook can run the test suite and refuse to let the agent finish while tests fail. The second is powerful and dangerous: an agent told it cannot stop until tests pass may try to change the tests. Use it only when the deny rules and guard from this block protect tests/.
crumbs: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates

title: Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions, hooks and review gates
text:
Data governance
A deny rule on reading a file stops the agent’s read tool. It does not stop R code or a shell command that reads the file and prints its contents, and anything printed enters the model’s context and is sent to the provider. Restricting tools reduces accidental exposure. It does not make an agent safe for confidential data. For personal or confidential data, work on a synthetic copy and run the final code yourself, outside the agent’s workspace.
Hooks and project settings are also code that runs on your machine. A cloned repository can carry its own settings and hooks, which is why Posit Assistant asks you to trust a workspace before using them. Trust only repositories whose configuration you have read.

The edit is blocked, because the hook could not approve itThe edit goes ahead: hooks fail open, so a crashing hook is treated as allowing the callThe agent stops and waits until jsonlite is installedThe edit is blocked only in plan mode

Which control detects a change to raw data made by any route?

A Claude Code Edit deny ruleA PreToolUse hook that searches for the pathA checksum test or git status, because they inspect the file itself rather than the action that changed itAn instruction in AGENTS.md

Hooks do not run for R codeThe guard matches the text 'data/raw', and the call never contains that texthere::here() runs with administrator rightsThe hook was registered for the wrong event

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
The repository layout
Cleaning is where an AI assistant looks most useful and where its mistakes are hardest to see. A cleaning script can run without error, return the right columns and produce plausible values while having treated a missing-value code as a measurement, kept the same animal twice, or dropped a row nobody noticed. None of these raises an error.
This block treats cleaning as four artefacts, each with a different owner:
You will work on a version of the voles data with errors planted in it. Your instructor holds the answer key, so at the end you can measure what your pipeline caught and what it missed.
⏱ ~75 minutes
The skill folder is stored once, in .agents/skills/, which Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot both read. Claude Code reads .claude/skills/ and follows symbolic links, so a link avoids keeping two copies. On macOS or Linux, from the repository root:
On Windows, symbolic links in git need extra configuration. Copying the folder is acceptable, but you then have two copies to keep in step.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 0: Lock the raw data
Everything later depends on the raw file being exactly what the data provider sent. Three controls protect it, and each covers a different route. The enforced-controls block explains each in more depth.
1. Record a checksum and commit it. Run this once, yourself:

raw_path <- here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")
writeLines(
  unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)),
  here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")
)

Add this line to .gitattributes so git does not convert line endings, which would change the checksum on Windows:
data/raw/** -text
2. Deny edits in the agent’s configuration. For Claude Code, the project file .claude/settings.json contains:
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)",
      "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/functions/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/**)"
    ]
  }
}
A leading / anchors each pattern to the project root. Run /permissions to confirm the rules are active. Posit Assistant has no documented path rules for file edits; use the guard hook from the enforced-controls block instead.
3. Test the control, do not assume it. Ask the agent to add a comment line to the top of data/raw/voles_raw.csv. It should be refused. Then run the tests (Step 5) and confirm the checksum test still passes.






Warning



What each control covers. The permission rule blocks the agent’s file-editing tools. It does not cover commands the agent runs through the shell or R: an R script that the agent runs is a different route. The checksum test catches a change made by any route, but only after the fact. On the Copilot cloud agent, where you have no local permission file, the checksum test running in CI plus branch protection is your control. Use both where you can: one prevents, the other detects.








Note



Data governance. A deny rule on editing does not stop data reaching the model provider. If the agent runs a script that prints data, those values enter its context. For personal or confidential data, let the agent work on a synthetic copy and run the final script on the real data yourself, outside the agent’s workspace.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
section: Step 1: Profile the raw data (R, not AI)
text:
Step 1: Profile the raw data (R, not AI)
Profiling is counting, and counting is something you should compute rather than ask a model to estimate. Run the provided script yourself:

# scripts/00_profile.R ----
# Purpose: describe the raw file as entered, before any decision is made.
# Every column is read as character so codes such as 9999 or -1 appear
# exactly as entered.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

raw_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

# one row per column: missingness, distinct values, numeric range ----
profile_df <- raw_df |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |>
  # suppressWarnings: text values become NA here by design
  mutate(value_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value))) |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    n_distinct = n_distinct(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_numeric = sum(!is.na(value_num)),
    min_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else min(value_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else max(value_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = column
  )

# every distinct label in the categorical columns ----
labels_df <- raw_df |>
  select(sex, treatment_arm) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |>
  count(column, value, sort = TRUE)

# identifiers that appear more than once ----
repeated_ids_df <- raw_df |>
  count(subject_id) |>
  filter(n > 1)

print(profile_df, n = Inf)
print(labels_df, n = Inf)
print(repeated_ids_df)

Keep the output. It is the factual input to Step 2.

section: Step 2: Draft the codebook, then audit it
text:
Step 2: Draft the codebook, then audit it


Draft and audit the codebook


1. Let the AI draft it from the profile alone. Do not give it the data provider’s note yet.
Here is a profile of a raw data file. Draft docs/codebook.csv with the
columns: column, type, rule, min, max, missing_codes, unit, source.
In the source column, state for every entry whether it comes from the
profile or is your assumption. Do not write any other file.

[paste the output of scripts/00_profile.R]
2. Audit the draft. Before you open docs/data_note.md, answer:

Did the draft list 9999 as a missing-value code, or treat it as a large measurement?
Did it notice that -1 is a code?
Where did its min and max come from? A range read off the data includes the errors in the data, so it cannot be used to detect them. Valid ranges must come from the biology or the protocol.

3. Correct it against the data provider’s note. Open docs/data_note.md and edit the codebook yourself. Every line should be traceable to the note or to a decision you can defend.




A codebook you could converge on

column,type,rule,min,max,missing_codes,unit,source
subject_id,character,"pattern ^V[0-9]{3}$; unique; pad digits to three",,,,,data note
sex,character,"allowed M, F; recode male to M, female to F",,,,,data note
treatment_arm,character,"allowed Control, Low_dose, High_dose; match case-insensitively",,,,,data note
mass_pre_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records)
mass_post_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records)
metabolic_rate_post,double,,5,30,-1,<unit>,data note (range from equipment)

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
section: Step 4: Clean with the skill, plan first
text:
Step 4: Clean with the skill, plan first
The skill holds the procedure; the codebook holds the facts. It sets disable-model-invocation: true, so it runs only when you invoke it by name. That is appropriate for a workflow that writes files.






Note.agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md





---
name: clean-with-codebook
description: >-
  Writes or revises a reproducible R cleaning script that applies a
  human-authored codebook (docs/codebook.csv) to raw tabular data. Use when
  asked to clean, recode or prepare raw data in a project that has a codebook.
  Not for exploratory analysis or modelling.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Clean data against a codebook

## Hard constraints
1. Never modify anything under data/raw/. Read raw files with explicit
   column types.
2. The codebook is the only source of rules. Do not infer units, ranges,
   missing-value codes or label mappings that the codebook does not state.
3. Do not edit docs/, scripts/functions/, scripts/02_validate.R,
   scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R or anything under tests/. If a check fails,
   report it; never change a check to make it pass.
4. Never drop a row silently. Every excluded row goes in the exclusion log
   with a reason.
5. Every changed cell goes in the cleaning log.
6. A value outside a codebook range that no codebook rule explains is set to
   NA, logged with rule "out_of_range_query", and listed in the final report.
   Never correct it by guessing a unit or decimal error.
7. No imputation.
8. Tidyverse style, native pipe, here::here() for all paths.

## Procedure
1. Present a plan before writing anything: every rule you will apply, the
   codebook row it comes from, and the order. Wait for the user to confirm.
2. If the data contain a value the codebook does not cover, stop and ask.
3. Write scripts/01_clean.R and run it in a fresh R session.
4. Run scripts/02_validate.R on the clean data and run the tests in tests/.
   Report the results verbatim.

## Outputs (exact columns)
- data/derived/voles_clean.csv: the codebook columns plus raw_row, the row
  number in the raw file.
- data/derived/exclusion_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, reason.
- data/derived/cleaning_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, column, old_value,
  new_value, rule.

## Final report
Row counts in, out and excluded; every value set to NA for query; any gaps
in the codebook you found.





Plan, review, then execute


1. With your repository committed and clean, switch your assistant to plan mode (in Posit Assistant, /plan; in Claude Code, plan mode) and invoke the skill:
/clean-with-codebook
Clean data/raw/voles_raw.csv using docs/codebook.csv. Start with the plan.
2. Review the plan before approving it. Check that:

every rule cites a codebook row;
out-of-range values are set to NA and queried, not “corrected”;
no file outside scripts/01_clean.R and data/derived/ will be written;
duplicates are handled by a stated rule, with each exclusion logged.

3. Approve, let it execute, and note every time it stopped to ask you something. A well-behaved agent should stop at least once.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 5: Check the result
Four checks, each catching something the others cannot.
1. Validation on clean data should pass. Run validate_voles() on data/derived/voles_clean.csv.
2. The tests: raw data unchanged and every row accounted for.

# tests/test_cleaning.R ----
library(testthat)
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

read_chr <- function(...) {
  readr::read_csv(
    here::here(...),
    col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())
  )
}

test_that("raw data are unchanged", {
  recorded <- readLines(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt"))
  current <- unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")))
  expect_identical(current, recorded)
})

test_that("every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log", {
  raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")
  clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")
  excluded_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "exclusion_log.csv")

  expect_equal(nrow(raw_df), nrow(clean_df) + nrow(excluded_df))
  expect_setequal(
    c(clean_df$raw_row, excluded_df$raw_row),
    as.character(seq_len(nrow(raw_df)))
  )
  expect_false(any(is.na(excluded_df$reason) | excluded_df$reason == ""))
})

test_that("clean data pass every codebook rule", {
  clean_df <- readr::read_csv(
    here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"),
    col_types = voles_col_types()
  )
  agent <- validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data")
  expect_true(pointblank::all_passed(agent))
})

Run with testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_cleaning.R")).
3. Audit the logs against the data. The cleaning log was written by the agent, so check it rather than trust it:

# scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

to_long <- function(data, value_name) {
  data |>
    pivot_longer(
      -raw_row,
      names_to = "column",
      values_to = value_name,
      values_transform = as.character
    )
}

raw_long_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) |>
  mutate(raw_row = as.character(row_number())) |>
  to_long("raw_value")

clean_long_df <- read_csv(here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) |>
  to_long("clean_value")

cleaning_log_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

# 1. Truthful: every logged old value matches the raw file ----
untruthful_df <- cleaning_log_df |>
  left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
  filter(!map2_lgl(old_value, raw_value, identical))

# 2. Complete: every changed cell appears in the log ----
unlogged_df <- clean_long_df |>
  left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
  filter(!map2_lgl(clean_value, raw_value, identical)) |>
  anti_join(cleaning_log_df, by = c("raw_row", "column"))

untruthful_df
unlogged_df

# 3. What kinds of change were made ----
cleaning_log_df |> count(column, rule, sort = TRUE)

# 4. Ten logged changes to check by hand against the raw file ----
set.seed(2026)
cleaning_log_df |> slice_sample(n = 10)

untruthful_df and unlogged_df should both have zero rows. An unlogged change is the most dangerous outcome in this block: a value altered with no record. If a row appears, inspect it; a difference in number formatting is harmless, a changed value is not. For the ten sampled changes, open the raw file yourself and confirm each one.
4. Grade the pipeline against the planted errors. Your instructor will now release the answer key. For each planted error, record:








Planted error
Failed validation on raw?
Handled as intended?
In the log?








The first column measures your rules; the second measures the cleaning; the third measures the record. A planted error that passed validation on raw data is a hole in your codebook, whatever the cleaning did.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Debrief

Which planted errors did the AI’s first draft of the codebook miss before you gave it the data provider’s note? What does that say about who should own the codebook?
What did the agent do with the mass recorded in kilograms and the value ten times too large? If it “corrected” them, on whose authority? If the provider confirms a kilogram entry, the correction becomes a codebook rule you add, not something the script infers.
Which of your checks would have caught a script that set every mass to NA?
Once the clean output is right, freeze it as a reference, as in the characterisation-test block, so a later refactor of 01_clean.R must reproduce it exactly.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Check your understanding
Why must the codebook be written or confirmed by the analyst rather than inferred by the AI from the data?

Because AI tools cannot read CSV filesBecause missing-value codes, units and valid ranges are facts about how the data were collected; ranges read off the data include the very errors they are meant to detectBecause codebooks must be written in a specific file formatBecause the AI would take too long to profile the data

Your validation rules all pass on the raw data before any cleaning. What is the most likely explanation in this exercise?

The cleaning script has already runpointblank cannot read raw dataThe rules have gaps, because the raw data are known to contain errorsThe data are clean and no cleaning is needed

How does the checksum test differ from the permission deny rule?

They are equivalent; one is redundantThe deny rule blocks one route (the agent's editing tools) before a change happens; the checksum detects a change by any route, after it happensThe checksum prevents edits; the deny rule only reports themThe deny rule works on GitHub; the checksum works only locally

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
References

Spreafico, M., Tassini, L., Sancricca, C. and Cappiello, C. (2025) ‘Lost in the pipeline: how well do large language models handle data preparation?’, arXiv preprint 2511.21708. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2511.21708

Claude Code documentation: Extend Claude Code, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/features-overview; Skills, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills; Configure permissions, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.
Posit Assistant documentation: Skills, https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/skills/.







NoteInstructor only: generating the planted data





Keep this script and planted_errors.csv outside the participant repository. An agent that can read the answer key will use it. Run it in an instructor copy of the repository that holds the clean data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv, and copy only the generated data/raw/voles_raw.csv into the participant repository.

# instructor/make_dirty_voles.R ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# suppressWarnings: case_when() evaluates every branch, including numeric
# conversion of text labels
as_num <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))

clean_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

plants_df <- tribble(
  ~row, ~column,               ~error_class,
  5,    "mass_post_g",         "sentinel 9999",
  41,   "mass_post_g",         "sentinel 9999",
  12,   "metabolic_rate_post", "non-standard missing code -1",
  20,   "treatment_arm",       "label in lower case",
  33,   "treatment_arm",       "label in upper case",
  58,   "sex",                 "label spelled out",
  27,   "mass_pre_g",          "recorded in kg",
  64,   "mass_pre_g",          "decimal slip (x10)"
) |>
  mutate(
    subject_id = clean_df$subject_id[row],
    old_value = map2_chr(row, column, \(r, col) clean_df[[col]][[r]]),
    new_value = case_when(
      error_class == "sentinel 9999" ~ "9999",
      error_class == "non-standard missing code -1" ~ "-1",
      error_class == "label in lower case" ~ str_to_lower(old_value),
      error_class == "label in upper case" ~ str_to_upper(old_value),
      error_class == "label spelled out" ~ if_else(old_value == "M", "male", "female"),
      error_class == "recorded in kg" ~ as.character(as_num(old_value) / 1000),
      error_class == "decimal slip (x10)" ~ as.character(as_num(old_value) * 10)
    )
  )

# apply each plant to its cell ----
planted_df <- reduce(
  seq_len(nrow(plants_df)),
  \(data, i) {
    data[[plants_df$column[[i]]]][[plants_df$row[[i]]]] <- plants_df$new_value[[i]]
    data
  },
  .init = clean_df
)

# insert an exact duplicate and a near duplicate with a malformed ID ----
near_duplicate_df <- planted_df |>
  slice(15) |>
  mutate(subject_id = str_replace(subject_id, "^V0", "V"))

raw_df <- bind_rows(
  slice(planted_df, 1:30),
  slice(planted_df, 7),
  slice(planted_df, 31:50),
  near_duplicate_df,
  slice(planted_df, 51:n())
)

write_csv(raw_df, here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), na = "")

# answer key, indexed by row in the raw file ----
key_df <- plants_df |>
  mutate(
    raw_row = row + (row > 30) + (row > 50),
    expected_handling = case_when(
      str_starts(error_class, "sentinel") |
        str_starts(error_class, "non-standard") ~ "recode to NA (codebook missing code); log",
      str_starts(error_class, "label") ~ "recode to canonical label; log",
      .default = "fails range rule; set to NA and query, do not infer a correction; log"
    )
  ) |>
  select(raw_row, subject_id, column, old_value, new_value, error_class, expected_handling) |>
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      raw_row = c(31, 52),
      subject_id = clean_df$subject_id[c(7, 15)],
      column = "(whole row)",
      error_class = c("exact duplicate row", "near duplicate: malformed ID"),
      expected_handling = c(
        "exclude one copy; log reason",
        "fails ID pattern; identify as duplicate of the original animal; exclude; log reason"
      )
    )
  )

write_csv(key_df, here("instructor", "planted_errors.csv"))

The raw file has 74 rows: 72 animals, one exact duplicate (raw row 31) and one near duplicate (raw row 52). A correct pipeline excludes two rows and sets five values to NA: two sentinels, the -1 code, and the two masses queried as out of range. These are in addition to the genuine missing value already in the source data.
docs/data_note.md should state: IDs are V followed by three digits; sex is M or F; the three treatment arms; masses in grams, with adults in this colony between 15 and 60 g and 9999 entered when an animal could not be weighed; metabolic rate -1 when the respirometry run failed, with valid readings between 5 and 30.
