title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Part 1: What AI is, and is not, good for in code review
⏱ ~90 minutes
⏱ ~15 minutes
The appeal of an AI reviewer is speed and coverage: it reads every line and does not tire. The danger is fluent, confident output that is sometimes wrong, in the same tone whether it is right or wrong.
Map its likely strengths onto the four Rs of code review (Ivimey-Cook et al., 2023):
AI capability mapped onto the four Rs

R
AI is likely to be...
Why



Reported
Useful for drafting
It can summarise what the script appears to do and flag missing documentation or undocumented exclusions. It cannot know the intended analysis unless you state it.


Run
Strong, if it can execute
An agent that runs the script in a fresh R session can show whether it runs. A chat window can only predict, and its prediction can read as though it ran the code.


Reliable
Weak
Silent semantic errors (P4 precedence, P8 sentinel, P9 incomparable models, P10 wrong family) depend on context. Expect some caught, some missed and some invented, all in the same confident tone.


Reproducible
Mixed
It can flag a missing lockfile or session record. It can confirm that results reproduce only by running the code and comparing outputs.
What the evidence says, and does not say. In an industrial study of an LLM-based review tool, about three-quarters of the automated comments were marked as resolved by developers, and most practitioners reported only a minor improvement in code quality (Cihan et al., 2025). A companion experiment by the same group found that review performance dropped when the model was not given a description of what the code was meant to do (Cihan, 2025, master’s thesis). Both studies concern software engineering, not statistical analysis scripts. No study we know of measures AI review of analysis code like ANALYSIS.R, which is why you will measure it yourself in Part 3.
The practical rule: treat every AI finding as a claim to verify, and treat the absence of a finding as no evidence that the problem is absent.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Tip



Opening poll (type in chat)
“If an AI code reviewer told you your analysis was clean, would you trust it enough to submit?”
A: Yes, it read every line B: Only if I had also read it myself C: No, I would trust my own review over the AI’s D: I would trust it for Run, not for Reliable
Keep the result visible; we return to it at the end.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
section: Part 2: Telling the AI how to behave
text:
Part 2: Telling the AI how to behave
⏱ ~20 minutes
A vague prompt (“review my code”) tends to produce a vague, generous review. Give the AI the same scaffold you used in the manual review.
The four things a review prompt should contain


A role and a standard. For example: “You are a critical code reviewer for an ecology journal applying the four Rs (Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible).” This gives the output a structure you can check.

The intended analysis. The AI cannot judge Reported or Reliable without knowing what the code is meant to do. State the model from the OSF page: TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | B), where TO is a count. Without this, it cannot know that a Gaussian lmer() is the wrong family (P10).

An instruction against flattery. “Do not praise. For each issue give the line number, the R it violates, the severity, and a concrete fix.” Check the output for praise anyway; the instruction is a request.

A demand for honest uncertainty. “Flag anything you cannot determine by reading alone as NEEDS HUMAN CHECK, rather than guessing.”



Activity: write the review prompt (10 minutes)


Write a prompt containing all four elements. The room splits in two for a controlled comparison:


Group A includes the line about the 9999 sentinel in the skeleton below.

Group B deletes it.

Everything else stays the same.


Working draft

You are a critical code reviewer for an evolutionary-biology journal.
Review ANALYSIS.R using the four Rs: Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible.

The intended analysis (from the pre-registration) is:
  total offspring (TO, a count: non-negative integer, often overdispersed)
  modelled as TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | block), with block as a random effect.

Rules:
- Do NOT praise the code. Report only problems.
- For each issue: line number(s), which R it violates, severity
  (critical / high / medium), and a concrete one-line fix.
- The raw data use 9999 as a "not recorded" code. Check whether this is
  handled.                                      <- Group B: delete this line
- Flag anything you CANNOT determine by reading alone as "NEEDS HUMAN
  CHECK" rather than guessing.
- If you are uncertain about a finding, say so explicitly.
Organise your output by the four Rs.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Part 3: Running the review
⏱ ~35 minutes
Path A: a local agent, read-only
Use Claude Code in plan mode, Posit Assistant in Ask mode, or Copilot Chat in Ask. At this rung the agent can read every file in the project but cannot change any, which is what a review needs.

Open the whole OSF project folder, so the agent can see the data files as well as ANALYSIS.R.
Give it your Part 2 prompt.
Save its review to a file of your own before moving on.
Path A, step 2: let it run the script (optional)
An agent that can execute R can turn the Run question from a prediction into evidence. Switch to rung 3 (acting with approval) and ask:
Run ANALYSIS.R from a fresh R session with Rscript and report the exact
output and any errors. Do not install packages; if a package is missing,
report which one. Do not edit any file.
Read the approval prompt before approving the command, and read the output it reports. If it says “the script runs”, find the command it ran and the output it saw. A claim that the script runs, with no command and no output, is a prediction. Missing packages on your machine are a finding about the environment, not about the code.
Path B: chat window
If you have no agent, paste the whole of ANALYSIS.R into any chat window, followed by your Part 2 prompt.






Warning



The chat window’s failure mode. A chat window cannot run anything. Asked “does this code run?”, it will produce a fluent answer that can read as though it executed the code. It did not. Ask instead “what would prevent this running?”, and treat any claim about reproduced results as unsupported.


Path C: Copilot code review on a pull request (demonstration)
If your repository is on GitHub, open a pull request containing ANALYSIS.R and request Copilot as a reviewer. Its comments appear on the changed lines, like a colleague’s. It reads the repository’s custom instructions, so the review conventions you wrote in the instructions-and-skills block apply.


Activity: grade the machine (20 minutes)


Open your P1–P12 catalogue beside the AI’s review and score it:


Hits: which of P1–P12 did it identify correctly?

Misses: which did it miss? Look especially at P4 (precedence) and P8 (sentinel), the silent, consequential ones.

False positives: what did it flag that is not a real problem, or describe wrongly?

Execution claims: did it claim the script runs or reproduces? On what evidence?

Post your group (A or B), your hit count, your most consequential miss and your most confident false positive in the chat, with line numbers.








Note



Debrief (5 minutes)

Compare P8 hit rates between Group A and Group B. The script alone does not reveal that 9999 is a code; the data and your knowledge do. What does that say about reviewing code without the data?
Whose AI produced the most confident false positive? A missed bug you may catch later; a fabricated one wastes review time and erodes trust in the tool.
Did any agent claim the script runs without having run it?
Return to the opening poll. Would you change your answer?

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
section: Part 4: Generating the README with AI
text:
Part 4: Generating the README with AI
⏱ ~20 minutes
The second deliverable is the documentation that makes Reported and Run answerable: a README. You are provided with the research-readme skill: a SKILL.md, two helper scripts and a template.
You run this in two passes. The first shows the failure; the second shows the fix.
Pass 1: README from the AI alone (demonstration, ~4 minutes)
Give the AI only ANALYSIS.R and the data, and ask for a README with no constraints. The result reads as complete. It will assign plausible units, describe variables it cannot have verified, and may state package versions it has no way to know. Note what it asserts about the variables and dependencies; Pass 2 replaces each guess with a fact you generate.
Pass 2: README from verifiable inputs
The skill’s rules are that the AI must not fabricate metadata, and that automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. So you generate the facts mechanically, and the AI only assembles and phrases them.
Step 1: Generate the inputs yourself (R, not AI)

skill_dir <- here::here(".agents", "skills", "research-readme", "scripts")

source(file.path(skill_dir, "describe_csv.R"))
describe_project_csvs(here::here())   # type, missing count and range per column

source(file.path(skill_dir, "scan_packages.R"))
print_lockfile(here::here("renv.lock"))  # R and package versions, or a finding

This project has no renv.lock. scan_packages.R reports that as an explicit finding rather than an error, and the README must say so. You cannot pin versions you never recorded.
Look at the offspring column in the summary: its range will read something like 2 to 9999. The 9999 code (P8) is a real number in the file, and the summary reports it without judgement. Judging plausibility is your job. That honest, uninterpreted range is the visible trace of the sentinel.
Step 2: Hand the AI the specification and the inputs
Agent path: invoke /research-readme and let its five stages run. It will ask you for what it cannot find.
Chat path: paste the structure from references/readme_template.md and the output you just generated, with this prompt:
Draft a research README.md for this analysis repository, using exactly the
sections in the template I paste below, in order.

Use ONLY the facts I provide. Do not invent DOIs, ORCIDs, units or package
versions. Where a value is missing, insert a visible placeholder:
  <!-- TODO: supply [field]: not provided -->

Per-column summaries: [paste describe_project_csvs() output]
Dependencies: [paste print_lockfile() output]
Run order: 01_data_cleaning.R, then 02_analysis.R.

Add an AI declaration stating that an AI assisted in drafting this README,
naming the model and today's date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere.


Activity: audit the README (10 minutes)


Audit the draft against three of the skill’s rules:


No fabrication. Pick three facts. Can you trace each to an input you gave? If not, it is invented.

Describe, do not interpret. Did the AI assign units or meanings you did not supply? Did the 2 to 9999 range survive, or was it “tidied” into something plausible and wrong?

README only. Confirm with git status that nothing except README.md changed.

Post the worst fabrication or interpretation you caught, and say whether the README’s offspring range alone would have led you back to P8.


The skill bundle
The bundle is reproduced here for reference; you do not edit it during the session. It lives in .agents/skills/research-readme/, linked into .claude/skills/ for Claude Code as described in the instructions-and-skills block.
research-readme/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   ├── describe_csv.R
│   └── scan_packages.R
└── references/
    └── readme_template.md






Notescripts/describe_csv.R






# describe_csv.R ----
# Purpose: one row per column of a CSV file: name, the type readr assigns,
# missing-value count, and a brief range (numeric) or distinct-value count
# (other). Describes; does not interpret.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 2.

describe_range <- function(x) {
  if (all(is.na(x))) {
    return("all values missing")
  }
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    return(paste(min(x, na.rm = TRUE), "to", max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
  }
  paste(dplyr::n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE), "distinct values")
}

# one-row-per-column summary of a single CSV ----
describe_csv <- function(path) {
  stopifnot(is.character(path), length(path) == 1L, file.exists(path))
  data_df <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  tibble::tibble(
    file        = basename(path),
    column      = names(data_df),
    type        = purrr::map_chr(data_df, \(x) class(x)[1]),
    n_missing   = purrr::map_int(data_df, \(x) sum(is.na(x))),
    range       = purrr::map_chr(data_df, describe_range),
    # completed by the user during Stage 2:
    description = NA_character_,
    unit        = NA_character_
  )
}

# describe every CSV in a project, skipping renv and git folders ----
describe_project_csvs <- function(project_dir) {
  stopifnot(dir.exists(project_dir))
  csv_paths <- list.files(
    project_dir,
    pattern = "\\.csv$",
    recursive = TRUE,
    full.names = TRUE,
    ignore.case = TRUE
  )
  csv_paths <- csv_paths[!grepl("(^|/)(renv|\\.git)/", csv_paths)]
  if (length(csv_paths) == 0L) {
    message("No CSV files found under ", project_dir)
    return(tibble::tibble())
  }
  csv_paths |>
    purrr::map(describe_csv) |>
    purrr::list_rbind()
}










Notescripts/scan_packages.R






# scan_packages.R ----
# Purpose: read renv.lock and report the R version and pinned package
# versions. A missing lockfile is reported as a finding, not an error.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 4.

read_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  if (!file.exists(lock_path)) {
    return(list(found = FALSE, r_version = NA_character_, packages = tibble::tibble()))
  }
  lock <- jsonlite::read_json(lock_path)
  packages <- purrr::pluck(lock, "Packages", .default = list())

  packages_df <- tibble::tibble(
    package = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Package", .default = NA_character_))),
    version = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Version", .default = NA_character_)))
  ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(package)

  list(
    found = TRUE,
    r_version = purrr::pluck(lock, "R", "Version", .default = NA_character_),
    packages = packages_df
  )
}

print_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  info <- read_lockfile(lock_path)
  if (!info$found) {
    cat(
      "No lockfile found at ", lock_path, ".\n",
      "FINDING: package versions were not recorded.\n",
      "README text: <!-- TODO: supply R version and key package versions: ",
      "not recorded; resolve before submission -->\n",
      sep = ""
    )
    return(invisible(info))
  }
  cat("R version: ", info$r_version, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(info$packages, n = Inf)
  invisible(info)
}










NoteSKILL.md





---
name: research-readme
description: >-
  Writes a README.md for a research repository whose code and data accompany
  a paper. Use when asked to write a README for an analysis project, document
  a repository for a paper, or prepare code for journal submission or
  archiving (Zenodo, Figshare, OSF). Not for general software READMEs and not
  for auditing code.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Research README generator

Produces one README.md for a repository of R code and data that accompanies a
manuscript, including the metadata that journals and archives expect:
persistent identifiers, ORCIDs, funding, per-variable descriptions with units,
an explicit script run order, and a dependency record.

## Operating constraints
These hold for the whole conversation unless the user explicitly withdraws
them.
1. The only file you create or overwrite is README.md. Do not edit, rename or
   delete any other file. If you notice an apparent error in code or data,
   record it under "Open questions" in the README or report it in chat, and
   leave the file untouched.
2. Do not fabricate metadata. DOIs, ORCIDs, grant numbers, collection dates,
   units and affiliations come from the user or from a file the user points to.
   If a value is unknown, insert a placeholder (see Placeholders).
3. Automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. Report column type,
   missing count and range. Do not state what a variable means, its unit, or
   whether a value is plausible.
4. Work conversationally and write the file directly; do not build an app.

## Before executing
Present a short numbered plan: the folder to be scanned, that only README.md
will be written, and the five stages below. Wait for the user to confirm.

## Stage 1: Project information
Collect title, abstract, DOIs (paper; archived code and data), licences,
authors with ORCIDs and affiliations, and funders with grant numbers. Read
these from CITATION.cff, codemeta.json or DESCRIPTION if present, and ask only
for what is missing. Pair each author with their own ORCID and affiliation. If
no code licence is supplied, flag it prominently and use a placeholder; do not
choose a licence for the user.

## Stage 2: Files and variable summaries
List the data and code files. For CSV files, run
describe_project_csvs() from scripts/describe_csv.R and use its output as a
scaffold. Ask the user for each column's description and unit, and for
collection dates and locations per data file. List other tabular formats
(.xlsx, .tsv) and ask the user to describe their columns by hand. Never infer
units from column names.

## Stage 3: Script order
List executable files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd). Propose a run order using numeric
prefixes (01_, 02_) as the first signal, and ask the user to confirm or
reorder; the user's order is authoritative. Collect a one-line description of
each script. Do not run any script to determine the order.

## Stage 4: R packages and versions
Run print_lockfile() from scripts/scan_packages.R.
- If a lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states the R version, says
  that versions are pinned in renv.lock, gives the restore command
  renv::restore(), and includes the package table.
- If no lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states that package versions
  were not recorded, and contains the placeholder from print_lockfile(). Do not
  guess versions or scan the installed library.

## Stage 5: Assemble, preview and reader-test
Fill references/readme_template.md. Show the rendered Markdown in chat. Then
read it as a newcomer who has only the repository and the paper: could they
find the data, restore the environment, run the scripts in order and
understand every variable? List any section still holding a placeholder. On
confirmation, write README.md to the project root.

## AI declaration
State that an AI assisted in generating this README, naming the model if the
user wishes, with the date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere in the
project unless the user states them, and then record exactly what they state.

## Placeholders
Write every unknown value as a visible placeholder, in exactly this form:
<!-- TODO: supply [field]: not provided -->
Flag a missing code licence and a missing code or data DOI as blocking for
submission, but still write the file so the user has a working draft.

## Scope
This skill does not audit code quality or reproducibility, and does not
produce figures. If asked to do either mid-run, say so and stop that part of
the request.

## References
- Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2023) Implementing code review in the scientific
  workflow. Journal of Evolutionary Biology 36(10), 1347–1356.
- Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2025) TADA! Simple guidelines to improve
  analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility. EcoEvoRxiv.









Notereferences/readme_template.md





The Dependencies section is a single token, filled with one of the two versions defined in Stage 4 of SKILL.md, so the README is accurate whether or not a lockfile exists.

text:
Check your understanding
An AI reviewer reports that ANALYSIS.R “runs without errors”. What do you need before treating that as evidence?

Nothing; the model has read every lineA second AI reviewer's agreementThe command it ran and the output it saw, from a fresh R session; without them the statement is a predictionA statement of confidence from the model

Why did Group A catch P8 more often than Group B?

Group A used a better modelNothing in the script reveals that 9999 is a code; the AI could only check for it when the prompt said soGroup B's prompt was longerP8 is a syntax error that only some models detect

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Glossary




Term
Definition



Agent
An AI that can read across a project's files and, depending on its mode, edit them and run commands, as opposed to a chat window that sees only pasted text


Read-only rung
A mode in which the assistant can read but not change anything: Claude Code plan mode, Posit Assistant Ask mode, Copilot Ask


False positive (in review)
A problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or is described wrongly


Claimed execution
A statement that code runs or reproduces, made without a command and its output to support it


Sentinel value
A number with a special meaning (9999 = not recorded); detectable from the data or from your instruction, not from the code alone


AI declaration
A README statement recording that an AI assisted, naming the model and date, and making no claims about AI use elsewhere

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
The repository layout
You have a computation that already works and you want to turn it into a reusable function. An agent can do that in seconds. The hard part is not the refactor but the verification: a change that “improves” code can quietly alter its output, so how do you confirm the function still does what the script did?
The method is to freeze the original result before anything is touched. You run the analysis once, save its output to a reference file (an .rds), and require the new function to reproduce that reference exactly. This is a characterisation test. It establishes that the output is unchanged, not that it is correct. Step 4 shows why that distinction matters, using a missing value that has been in the data all along.
The block has a shared spine and three paths that differ in who writes the function and the test:
All paths rejoin at Step 4.
⏱ ~60 minutes
The single most important property of this layout: the file tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds is created by you, once, and by nobody else. Every protection in this block exists to keep that true.

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
The original scripts
The data are read by one function that states every column type. The analysis, the reference and the test all call it, so they read the data identically. A column whose type read_csv() guesses differently in one place produces a test failure that has nothing to do with the refactor.

# scripts/functions/load_voles.R ----
load_voles <- function() {
  readr::read_csv(
    here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
    col_types = readr::cols(
      subject_id          = readr::col_character(),
      sex                 = readr::col_character(),
      treatment_arm       = readr::col_character(),
      mass_pre_g          = readr::col_double(),
      mass_post_g         = readr::col_double(),
      metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double()
    )
  )
}


# scripts/01_load_data.R ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))

voles <- load_voles()

Inspect the data with glimpse(voles) at the console, not inside the script, so that sourcing the script from a test prints nothing.

# scripts/02_analysis.R: the original, trusted version ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "01_load_data.R"))

metabolic_summary <- voles |>
  group_by(treatment_arm, sex) |>
  summarise(
    mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post),
    sd_rate   = sd(metabolic_rate_post),
    n         = n(),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

Two things to notice now and leave alone:

The data contain one missing value in metabolic_rate_post, and this code has no na.rm, so one cell of the result is NA. Do not “fix” it yet. Step 4 is about exactly this.

group_by() returns groups sorted by their keys. The .by argument returns them in order of first appearance in the data. If the two orders differ, a refactor that switches to .by changes the row order of the output.

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
section: Step 0 (spine): capture and protect the reference
text:
Step 0 (spine): capture and protect the reference
Before anything else, run scripts/02_analysis.R yourself and confirm that metabolic_summary looks as you expect, including the one NA cell. Then run the capture script once:

# tests/make_reference.R ----
# Run ONCE, by you, BEFORE any refactoring.
source(here::here("scripts", "02_analysis.R"))
dir.create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
saveRDS(
  metabolic_summary,
  here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds")
)

Commit the reference immediately, so that any later change to it is visible:
git add tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds
git commit -m "Capture reference output before refactoring"
Capture it now, before the refactor. Afterwards, 02_analysis.R computes the summary through the very function under test, so re-capturing would compare the function with itself.
Protect it. Each control covers a different route:


Local agent (Claude Code). Add deny rules to .claude/settings.json:
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/data/**)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)"
    ]
  }
}
Run /permissions to confirm the rules are active, then ask the agent to delete the .rds file and check that it is refused.


Asynchronous agent (Copilot). Add a .github/CODEOWNERS file naming yourself for the protected paths, and turn on branch protection for main so that merging requires your review and a passing r-checks run:
/tests/fixtures/      @your-github-username
/tests/make_reference.R @your-github-username
/.github/             @your-github-username

Every route. Git. git status --short tests/fixtures should print nothing for the rest of this block.







Warning



What a deny rule does not cover. Claude Code’s deny rules apply to its built-in file tools, not to commands it runs through the shell. An agent that ran Rscript tests/make_reference.R would overwrite your reference without touching an edit tool. That is why git, not the deny rule, is the final check, and why the checklists below ask you to read the agent’s command log.


You now hold the reference. Pick one path, then rejoin at Step 4.
crumbs: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
section: Path A: write the function and the test yourself
text:
Path A: write the function and the test yourself
A tidy refactor naturally reaches for the modern .by argument. Write this first attempt in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R:


First attempt (deliberately incomplete)


# scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: first attempt ----
summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post),
      sd_rate   = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post),
      n         = dplyr::n(),
      .by       = c(treatment_arm, sex)
    )
}


Now write the test and run it:

# tests/test_summary_functions.R ----
library(testthat)
local_edition(3)
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R"))

test_that("summarise_metabolic_rate() reproduces the original summary", {
  reference <- readRDS(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds"))
  expect_equal(summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()), reference, tolerance = 1e-8)
})

Run it with testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_summary_functions.R")).


What happened

It fails, and not on the numbers. .by returns the groups in order of first appearance; the reference, made with group_by(), has them sorted. The values are right but the rows are in a different order, and expect_equal() reports a mismatch. Add dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) to the end of the pipeline and the test passes. That failure is the lesson in miniature: a change that improved the code altered the output, and the characterisation test caught it.
If your test passed first time, the data happen to be stored in sorted order. Check with load_voles() |> dplyr::distinct(treatment_arm, sex).

While writing the test, resist one temptation: do not type the expected numbers into the test as literals. A test that compares the function with numbers you transcribed proves nothing about whether the refactor preserved the original computation. The test must read the .rds.
The function you should converge on, with documentation and an argument check:


Refactored function


# scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: refactored ----
#' Summarise post-treatment metabolic rate by treatment arm and sex
#'
#' @param data A data frame with columns treatment_arm, sex and
#'   metabolic_rate_post.
#' @return A tibble with one row per treatment_arm and sex, sorted by both,
#'   giving the mean, standard deviation and number of rows.
summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data))
  required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post")
  missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data))
  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(
      "`data` is missing required column(s): ",
      paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post),
      sd_rate   = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post),
      n         = dplyr::n(),
      .by       = c(treatment_arm, sex)
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)
}


Finally, make scripts/02_analysis.R call the function, so it genuinely replaces the code it came from:

# scripts/02_analysis.R: after refactoring ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "01_load_data.R"))
source(here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R"))

metabolic_summary <- summarise_metabolic_rate(voles)

Run the test again; it should still pass. Rejoin at Step 4.

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
section: Path B: a local agent, in two prompts
text:
Path B: a local agent, in two prompts
Use this path to let an agent do the work while you verify. Split the job into two prompts, not one. A single prompt that writes both the refactor and the test lets one misunderstanding (about row order, say) shape both files at once, producing a passing test that proves nothing. Separating them stops the test inheriting the refactor’s assumptions.
Prompt 1: the refactor only.
Move the computation in scripts/02_analysis.R into a documented function
summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, with a
roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 02_analysis.R call the new function
instead of the inline pipeline. Do not write any tests, and do not touch
anything under tests/.
Read what it writes. If it uses .by without a trailing arrange(), leave that for now; the next step will expose it.
Prompt 2: the test only.
Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source
scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R,
read tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds, and compare it with
summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) using expect_equal().

Do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/, and do not
run tests/make_reference.R. I captured that reference myself; a reference you
generate proves nothing.
Before you trust a passing test, check what the agent wrote and did:

The test reads tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds. It does not hard-code expected numbers. If it does, the check is circular whatever the result.
The test calls summarise_metabolic_rate(), the function under test, not a reimplementation of the pipeline inside the test.

git status --short tests/fixtures prints nothing.
The agent’s command log shows no run of tests/make_reference.R.

Now run the test yourself. If the function used .by without arrange(), it fails on row order, not values. Have the agent add dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) and run again. If it passed first time, remove the arrange() yourself to see the failure, then restore it. Rejoin at Step 4.

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
section: Path C: an asynchronous agent (Copilot cloud agent)
text:
Path C: an asynchronous agent (Copilot cloud agent)
The same work can be handed to an agent that runs remotely while you do something else. It works on a branch in GitHub’s infrastructure and returns a pull request. Before you start, check that your Copilot plan includes the coding agent, that copilot-setup-steps.yml is on your default branch, and that the CODEOWNERS file and branch protection from Step 0 are in place.
Keep the two-step discipline by writing two issues, and assign the second only after you have reviewed and merged the first.
Issue 1
Title: Move the metabolic-rate summary into a function

Move the summary computation in scripts/02_analysis.R into a documented
function summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R,
with a roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 02_analysis.R call it.

Acceptance criteria:
- Do not add or change anything under tests/, data/ or .github/.
- The output must be identical to the current output, including row order
  and the existing NA value.
Issue 2 (after Issue 1 is merged)
Title: Add a characterisation test for summarise_metabolic_rate()

Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source
scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, and
compare summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) with
tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds using expect_equal().

Acceptance criteria:
- Do not create, modify or regenerate anything under tests/fixtures/, and do
  not run tests/make_reference.R.
- Run the tests and report the result in the pull request description.
Assign each issue to Copilot. When a pull request arrives:

Open Files changed. Confirm that only the expected files changed. A change under tests/fixtures/ or .github/ should not merge, and CODEOWNERS will in any case require your review for it.
Read the test against the four-point checklist in Path B.
Check that the r-checks run on the pull request passed.
Pull the branch and run the test on your own machine. The agent’s report that “tests pass” is its claim; your run is the check.

If something is wrong, comment on the pull request to ask for a revision, or close it. Nothing reaches main until you merge.
crumbs: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
Step 4 (spine): unchanged is not correct
Your test passes. The function reproduces the reference exactly, including the NA cell. The characterisation test has certified that the refactor preserved the original behaviour, and the original behaviour reports a missing mean for one group of animals.
Is that the right answer? It depends on what you meant. If you want the mean of the animals that were measured, the original code was wrong all along, and the refactor faithfully preserved the error. A characterisation test cannot tell the difference, because it compares against the past, not against the truth.


Decide, change, and test the change independently


1. Decide. Suppose you conclude that the mean and standard deviation should use the measured animals only. There is a second, quieter problem: n() counts rows, including the animal with no measurement, so n would no longer match the number of values behind the mean. A summary that reports a mean of 11 animals beside n = 12 misstates the sample size.
2. Change the function (by hand or with your agent):


Changed function


# scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: missing values handled ----
summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data))
  required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post")
  missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data))
  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(
      "`data` is missing required column(s): ",
      paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_rate   = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_used    = sum(!is.na(metabolic_rate_post)),
      n_missing = sum(is.na(metabolic_rate_post)),
      .by       = c(treatment_arm, sex)
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)
}


3. Run the characterisation test. It fails, correctly. The output has changed, and the test exists to tell you so.
4. Add a known-answer test before re-capturing anything. A known-answer test checks the new behaviour against a result you can compute by hand, independent of any reference file:

# add to tests/test_summary_functions.R ----
test_that("means ignore missing values and n_used counts measured animals", {
  toy_df <- tibble::tibble(
    treatment_arm       = c("Control", "Control", "Control"),
    sex                 = c("F", "F", "F"),
    metabolic_rate_post = c(10, 14, NA)
  )
  result <- summarise_metabolic_rate(toy_df)

  expect_equal(result$mean_rate, 12)
  expect_equal(result$n_used, 2)
  expect_equal(result$n_missing, 1)
})

5. Only now, re-capture the reference, as a recorded decision. Re-run tests/make_reference.R yourself and commit with a message that states why:
git add tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds scripts/functions/summary_functions.R tests/test_summary_functions.R
git commit -m "Exclude missing metabolic rates from mean and SD; report n_used and n_missing"
Re-capturing compares the function with itself, so it is acceptable only under three conditions: you decided it, an independent known-answer test checks the new behaviour, and the commit records why. Without those, re-capturing a reference to make a failing test pass is the circular verification this whole block warns against.


The general rule: characterisation tests protect behaviour you have already judged correct. Judging it correct is a separate step, and it is yours.
crumbs: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
section: The environment the test runs in (spine)
text:
The environment the test runs in (spine)
A characterisation test is only as stable as the environment it runs in. The column types in load_voles() handle the finest-grained part. The R version and the package set are handled by two GitHub Actions workflows.
r-checks.yml is the independent check. It runs the tests from a clean checkout on every push to main and on every pull request:
name: r-checks
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: "4.5.2"   # match the R version in renv.lock
          use-public-rspm: true
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
      - name: Run tests
        run: Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests", stop_on_failure = TRUE)'
It is independent of your machine and of the agent’s environment, but it is not tamper-proof. A pull request can change the workflow file or the reference it checks against. CODEOWNERS and branch protection (Step 0) are what make a passing run meaningful: you review every change to those paths before it merges.
copilot-setup-steps.yml builds the environment the Copilot cloud agent works in. Following GitHub’s documented pattern:
name: "Copilot Setup Steps"

# Runs when this file changes, so you can see whether setup succeeds,
# and can be run by hand from the Actions tab.
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

jobs:
  # The job must be called copilot-setup-steps or Copilot will not use it.
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up R
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: "4.5.2"   # match the R version in renv.lock
          use-public-rspm: true
      - name: Restore packages from renv.lock
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
Four requirements, each with a different failure mode:


The job name must be exactly copilot-setup-steps. If it is not, Copilot ignores the file and works without your packages. That failure is usually loud: the tests error on the first missing function.

The file must be on the default branch, or it is not used.

The runner must be Ubuntu x64 Linux, the only runner type the cloud agent supports.

The lockfile must be restored. If it restores the wrong versions, the failure is quiet: tests run and pass against different package behaviour. The frozen reference then certifies sameness against the wrong baseline.

When the agent’s test run and the independent r-checks run disagree, suspect the environment before you suspect the code.
crumbs: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
From convention to skill
The protective sentence in Path B (“do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/”) is a durable convention: it is the same for every refactor. Anything you retype into every prompt is a candidate for a skill. A skill for this workflow would say: capture the reference only if the human has not; never regenerate a fixture; refactor and test in separate steps; compare against the human-held reference.
The benefit is that you stop retyping the boundary. The hazard is the same sentence read the other way: once the rule lives in a skill, you no longer see it, and a colleague using your skill may not know that the whole trust argument rests on it. A skill is also only an instruction. The deny rules, CODEOWNERS and git checks in this block hold whether or not the agent reads it. Build the skill only after you have done Path A or B, and keep the “reference stays with the human” clause as a visible line.
crumbs: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged

title: Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
Check your understanding
A characterisation test passes after a refactor. What has it established?

That the function's output is correctThat the function's output is the same as the original code's output, whether or not that output was correctThat the function is faster than the original codeThat the original code had no bugs

Why must the agent never generate the reference file?

Because agents cannot write .rds filesBecause the reference would be too largeBecause a reference produced by the code under test can only confirm that the code agrees with itselfBecause reference files must be written in a different language

You have added Edit deny rules for tests/fixtures/ in Claude Code. Which action could still change the reference?

Asking the agent to edit the .rds file with its editing toolThe agent running tests/make_reference.R through the shellOpening the .rds file in the IDERunning testthat::test_file() on the test file







NoteInstructor notes






Check your copy of voles_metabolism.csv before teaching: the .by failure in Path A appears only if load_voles() |> dplyr::distinct(treatment_arm, sex) is not already in sorted order. If it is sorted, reorder the rows of the file once and commit it before the session.
Confirm that the file contains exactly one missing value in metabolic_rate_post, and note which group it falls in, for the Step 4 discussion.
Path C depends on account features. Run it once on a participant-type account before the session.

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
text:
Part A: Simulation and parameter recovery
Earlier blocks checked that code runs, that data are clean, and that a refactor leaves results unchanged. None of those checks asks whether the statistical code estimates what you think it estimates. This block covers four checks for that, each built on the same division of labour:
⏱ ~70 minutes
⏱ ~25 minutes
If you simulate data from a mechanism whose parameters you chose, a correct analysis should recover those parameters on average, and its 95% confidence intervals should contain the true values about 95% of the time. This tests the analysis code against a known answer, which real data never provide.
Morris, White and Crowther (2019) give a structure for planning simulation studies: the aims, the data-generating mechanism, the estimand, the methods and the performance measures (ADEMP). Here:
The written mechanism is yours. It is the equivalent of the codebook in the data-cleaning block: the AI turns it into code, and you check the code against it.
crumbs: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
text:
Aim: check that the analysis code estimates the high-dose effect correctly.

Data-generating mechanism: 12 voles per arm-by-sex cell. Pre-treatment mass is normal with mean 28 g and SD 2 g. Post-treatment mass equals 2.8 g plus 0.9 times pre-treatment mass, plus 0.8 g for Low_dose, plus 1.5 g for High_dose, plus 1.0 g for males, plus normal error with SD 0.8 g.

Estimand: the difference in post-treatment mass between High_dose and Control, adjusted for pre-treatment mass and sex. True value: 1.5 g.

Method: linear model (ANCOVA), mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex.

Performance measures: bias and confidence-interval coverage, each with its Monte Carlo standard error.




Write, check, recover (25 minutes)


1. Simulation code. Give the AI the data-generating mechanism above, word for word, and ask for a function simulate_voles() returning a tibble with columns treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g and mass_post_g.
2. Check the simulated data against the specification. Before using the function, run it once and check that it matches what you wrote:

set.seed(1)
sim_df <- simulate_voles()
sim_df |> count(treatment_arm, sex)            # 12 per cell?
sim_df |> summarise(mean(mass_pre_g), sd(mass_pre_g))
sim_df |>
  summarise(mean_post = mean(mass_post_g), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex))

High_dose should be about 1.5 g above Control within each sex, and males about 1 g above females. If not, the simulation is wrong, and nothing built on it can be trusted.
3. Analysis code, in a separate session. Without showing it the simulation code, ask the AI for a function estimate_high_vs_control(data) that fits the model above and returns the High_dose estimate and its 95% confidence interval.
4. Run the recovery.


Reference code


simulate_voles <- function(n_per_cell = 12, effect_low = 0.8,
                           effect_high = 1.5, sex_effect = 1.0,
                           slope_pre = 0.9, sd_pre = 2, sd_resid = 0.8) {
  tidyr::expand_grid(
    treatment_arm = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"),
    sex = c("F", "M"),
    animal = seq_len(n_per_cell)
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      mass_pre_g = stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), mean = 28, sd = sd_pre),
      arm_effect = dplyr::case_when(
        treatment_arm == "Low_dose" ~ effect_low,
        treatment_arm == "High_dose" ~ effect_high,
        .default = 0
      ),
      mass_post_g = 28 * (1 - slope_pre) + slope_pre * mass_pre_g +
        arm_effect + sex_effect * (sex == "M") +
        stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), sd = sd_resid)
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g)
}

estimate_high_vs_control <- function(data) {
  data <- dplyr::mutate(
    data,
    treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"))
  )
  fit <- stats::lm(mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, data = data)
  ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
    lower = unname(ci[1]),
    upper = unname(ci[2])
  )
}



set.seed(2026)
n_sim <- 1000
true_effect <- 1.5

results_df <- seq_len(n_sim) |>
  map(\(i) estimate_high_vs_control(simulate_voles(effect_high = true_effect))) |>
  list_rbind()

results_df |>
  summarise(
    bias          = mean(estimate) - true_effect,
    bias_mcse     = sd(estimate) / sqrt(n_sim),
    coverage      = mean(lower <= true_effect & upper >= true_effect),
    coverage_mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_sim),
    empirical_se  = sd(estimate)
  )

Bias should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero. Coverage should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.95, roughly 0.936 to 0.964 with 1,000 runs.
5. Prove the check can fail. Replace the analysis with a version that models the change the wrong way round, as in the debugging block:

estimate_buggy <- function(data) {
  data <- dplyr::mutate(
    data,
    treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")),
    mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g
  )
  fit <- stats::lm(mass_change_g ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = data)
  ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
    lower = unname(ci[1]),
    upper = unname(ci[2])
  )
}

Rerun the recovery with estimate_buggy(). Bias should be about −3 g and coverage near zero. A check you have never seen fail is a check you are assuming works.








Warning



What recovery does not prove. It shows that the code estimates the right quantity under the mechanism you simulated. It says nothing about whether real voles behave like that. A change-score model fitted to these simulated data would also be nearly unbiased (randomisation makes both estimators valid), but less precise; compare empirical_se to see the cost. Recovery tests code, not scientific assumptions.
crumbs: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
section: Part B: Translation with an equivalence check
text:
Part B: Translation with an equivalence check
⏱ ~15 minutes
Translating code (base R to tidyverse, or SPSS, Stata or SAS to R) is a task AI does quickly. The characterisation-test idea applies directly: run both versions and compare the outputs.


Translate and compare (15 minutes)


1. Here is a short base R script:

voles <- read.csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
rate_mean <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex,
                       data = voles, FUN = mean)
rate_n <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex,
                    data = voles, FUN = length)
names(rate_n)[3] <- "n"
legacy_summary <- merge(rate_mean, rate_n, by = c("treatment_arm", "sex"))

2. Ask the AI to translate it into tidyverse code producing tidy_summary, with the same columns.
3. Compare. Normalise only presentation (type and row order), never values:

normalise <- function(data) {
  data |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(across(where(is.factor), as.character)) |>
    arrange(treatment_arm, sex)
}

testthat::expect_equal(normalise(tidy_summary), normalise(legacy_summary))

4. If the comparison fails after normalising, you have found a real difference in behaviour. Find it before reading on.


The difference

aggregate() with a formula drops rows with a missing value in any variable in the formula, silently. The one animal with no metabolic_rate_post is excluded from both the mean and the count. A direct translation using summarise(mean(metabolic_rate_post), n()) returns NA for that cell’s mean and counts the animal in n. Neither version is “the translation”; they make different decisions about missing data. Decide which you want, write it explicitly (na.rm = TRUE and a count of non-missing values), and record the decision. This is the same problem as the “unchanged is not correct” step of the characterisation-test block, reached from a different direction.



When translating from other software, you usually cannot run the original inside R. Export its results to a file, compare against those, and expect differences in defaults: how missing values are handled, how quantiles are defined, and how results are rounded. Each difference needs a decision, not a tolerance setting.
crumbs: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
text:
Part C: Robustness, not choice
⏱ ~15 minutes
AI should not choose your primary analysis. The BLADE benchmark compared language-model agents with expert analysts on open-ended research questions. It found that the models were often limited to basic analyses, and that agents able to explore the data made more varied but still sub-optimal analytical decisions (Gu et al., 2024). Its useful role is narrower: listing defensible alternatives to an analysis you have already fixed, so you can check whether your conclusion depends on the choice.


Enumerate, judge, run (15 minutes)


1. Ask for alternatives, not a recommendation:
My pre-registered primary analysis is an ANCOVA:
mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, estimating the High_dose
versus Control difference. List alternative specifications a reasonable
analyst might use for the same question, and for each, say whether it
estimates the same quantity. Do not recommend one.
2. Judge each one yourself. Mark it defensible or not, with a reason. Check especially whether the alternative estimates the same quantity.
3. Run the defensible ones and report them beside the primary analysis.

voles_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")))

specs_df <- tribble(
  ~spec,                       ~formula,
  "Primary: ANCOVA",           "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex",
  "Change score",              "I(mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) ~ treatment_arm + sex",
  "ANCOVA with arm-by-sex",    "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm * sex"
)

spec_results_df <- specs_df |>
  mutate(result = map(formula, \(f) {
    fit <- lm(as.formula(f), data = voles_df)
    ci <- confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
    tibble(
      estimate = unname(coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
      lower = unname(ci[1]),
      upper = unname(ci[2])
    )
  })) |>
  unnest(result)

spec_results_df



A trap in the table

In the third specification, the coefficient treatment_armHigh_dose is the High_dose effect in females only (the reference level of sex), because the model includes an interaction. It sits in the same column as the other estimates but answers a different question. It belongs in a separate analysis of whether the effect differs by sex, not in a table of estimates of the same quantity. An AI that lists it as an “alternative” without saying so has made exactly the error step 2 asks you to catch.









Warning



Running many specifications and reporting the one you like best is selective reporting. The primary analysis is fixed in advance; the others are reported as sensitivity analyses whatever they show.
crumbs: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
section: Part D: Reporting without typed numbers
text:
Part D: Reporting without typed numbers
⏱ ~10 minutes
A number typed into a report is a number that can be mistyped, or left unchanged when the data change. When an assistant drafts the text, it may also “helpfully” restate numbers it saw earlier in the conversation. Every number in the prose should come from inline code:

# in a chunk
primary <- spec_results_df |> filter(spec == "Primary: ANCOVA")

and in the text:
High-dose voles were `r round(primary$estimate, 2)` g heavier than controls
after treatment (95% CI `r round(primary$lower, 2)` to
`r round(primary$upper, 2)` g).
Your AGENTS.md should already say never to type numerical results into text. That is a request. This function is the check: it lists prose lines in a .qmd file that still contain numbers outside inline code, for you to review by eye.

find_typed_numbers <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
  is_fence <- grepl("^```", lines)
  in_chunk <- cumsum(is_fence) %% 2 == 1

  tibble(line = seq_along(lines), text = lines) |>
    filter(!in_chunk, !is_fence) |>
    mutate(prose = gsub("`\\{?r\\}? [^`]*`", "", text)) |>
    filter(grepl("[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+|\\b[0-9]{2,}\\b", prose, perl = TRUE)) |>
    select(line, text)
}

find_typed_numbers(here("report.qmd"))

It will also flag years, sample sizes from the design and the YAML header, so treat each hit as a question, not an error.
Record AI use as you go. Many journals, funders and institutions now ask authors to declare AI use. A short log written at the time is easier and more accurate than reconstruction later. One line per session is enough:
2026-10-09; Claude Code (model as reported in the session); translated
summary script to tidyverse; kept translation, changed missing-value
handling to na.rm = TRUE after equivalence check.
Check your institution’s and target journal’s current policy for what must be declared and where.
crumbs: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results

title: Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results
text:
Check your understanding
A simulation recovers the true effect with negligible bias and 95% coverage. What has it shown?

That the real data follow the simulated mechanismThat the analysis code estimates the intended quantity correctly when the data follow the simulated mechanismThat the study has adequate powerThat the model's assumptions hold for the real data

A translated script and the original disagree only after you convert factors to characters and sort the rows. What should you do next?

Increase the tolerance until the test passesAccept the translation, since the AI wrote itFind the behavioural difference (for example, missing-value handling), decide which behaviour is correct, and record the decisionRevert to the original script

Why should the arm-by-sex interaction model not appear in the same robustness table as the primary ANCOVA?

Interaction models cannot be fitted with lm()Its High_dose coefficient estimates the effect in the reference sex only, a different quantity from the primary estimandIt always gives a larger estimateRobustness tables may contain only two models
